title: Lenvatinib versus Placebo in Radioiodine-Refractory Thyroid Cancer (SELECT)
authors: Schlumberger M, Tahara M, Wirth LJ, Robinson B, et al.

pico.label: Population
pico.text: 392 adults in 21 countries (2011 to 2012) with measurable radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer and independently confirmed progression within the previous 13 months. 51% papillary, 12% poorly differentiated, 19% follicular, 18% Hürthle cell; 24% had received one previous tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

pico.label: Intervention
pico.text: Lenvatinib 24 mg once daily in 28-day cycles (n = 261), with dose reductions to 20, 14 or 10 mg for toxicity.

pico.label: Comparator
pico.text: Placebo (n = 131), with open-label lenvatinib allowed after centrally confirmed progression.

pico.label: Outcome
pico.text: Primary: progression-free survival by blinded independent radiological review. Secondary: response rate, overall survival and safety.

bottom: Lenvatinib extended median progression-free survival from 3.6 to 18.3 months in progressive radioiodine-refractory disease (HR 0.21, 99% CI 0.14 to 0.31), with responses in 64.8%, across all histologies and whether or not a previous kinase inhibitor had been used. The full paper shows a heavy toxicity burden: 75.9% had grade 3 or worse treatment-related events, two-thirds needed dose reductions, and 6 deaths were judged drug-related. Overall survival was not improved (HR 0.73), as almost all placebo patients crossed over. Strong evidence of disease control in patients with progressive disease, but not a reason to start treatment in stable, asymptomatic disease.

appraisal.heading: The question
appraisal.text: Radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer has a 10-year survival of about 10% from detection of metastases, and until 2013 there was no effective systemic treatment. Sorafenib (DECISION) had improved progression-free survival by about 5 months. Lenvatinib inhibits VEGF receptors and also FGF receptors, RET, KIT and PDGFR, and had shown activity in phase 2. SELECT tested it against placebo.

appraisal.heading: Who and where
appraisal.text: An international collaboration led from Gustave Roussy, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Funded by Eisai, which designed the study with the principal investigators; data were managed by a contract research organisation, Eisai statisticians did the analysis and Eisai-funded medical writers helped draft the paper. Registered as NCT01321554.

appraisal.heading: Design and methods
appraisal.text: Double-blind phase 3 trial with 2:1 central block randomisation, stratified by age, region and previous kinase inhibitor. Progression had to be confirmed by independent review before entry, which is unusual and strengthens the population definition. Progression-free survival was assessed by blinded central review every 8 weeks. Powered (90%, two-sided alpha 0.01) for an HR of 0.57, assuming medians of 14 versus 8 months, needing 214 events. Overall survival was analysed unadjusted and with a rank-preserving structural failure time model to correct for crossover.

appraisal.heading: Results
appraisal.text: Median follow-up about 17 months. Events 220. Median progression-free survival 18.3 months (95% CI 15.1 to not estimable) versus 3.6 months (2.2 to 3.7); HR 0.21 (99% CI 0.14 to 0.31). Progression-free at 12 months 63.0% versus 10.5%. Benefit held in every prespecified subgroup, including previous kinase inhibitor (median 15.1 months) and all histologies, and regardless of BRAF or RAS status. Response 64.8% (4 complete) versus 1.5%; median time to response 2.0 months. Overall survival HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.50 to 1.07, P = 0.10); crossover-adjusted HR 0.62 (0.40 to 1.00). 109 of 114 placebo patients with progression (95.6%) crossed over. Treatment-related grade 3 or worse adverse events 75.9% versus 9.9%: hypertension 41.8% grade 3 or worse, proteinuria 10.0%. Dose reductions 67.8%, interruptions 82.4%, mean daily dose 17.2 mg. Fatal adverse events 20 (7.7%) versus 6 (4.6%), of which 6 on lenvatinib were judged treatment-related.

appraisal.heading: Strengths
points: Double-blind and placebo-controlled, with blinded independent review of progression.
Entry required independently confirmed progression, so the population had genuinely active disease.
A very large effect, consistent across histology, mutation status and previous treatment, and robust in sensitivity analyses.

appraisal.heading: Weaknesses and bias
points: Progression-free survival, not overall survival, is the primary endpoint. Survival was not significantly improved, though crossover makes this hard to interpret.
The placebo arm progressed much faster than assumed (3.6 versus 8 months), which inflates the hazard ratio compared with what might be seen in less aggressive disease.
Substantial toxicity: most patients needed dose reductions and the mean dose was 17.2 mg, so 24 mg is a starting dose few patients sustain.
Blinding is likely to have been compromised by hypertension, proteinuria and other on-target effects.
No quality-of-life data in the main paper.
Sponsor ran the statistics and funded writing support; the sponsor-designed protocol was shared with the principal investigators.

appraisal.heading: What the abstract does not tell you
appraisal.text: That the placebo arm did far worse than the trial assumed. That two-thirds needed dose reductions and the average dose was 17.2 mg. That 7.7% died of adverse events during treatment, 6 judged drug-related. That nearly all placebo patients crossed over, so the trial cannot answer whether lenvatinib prolongs life. The Kaplan-Meier plot shows half the placebo arm progressing within about 4 months, confirming how aggressive the disease was. Bone metastasis progression, the subgroup forest plots, adverse event management and the crossover model are in the supplementary appendix, which was not read.

appraisal.heading: How it changed practice
appraisal.text: SELECT made lenvatinib the first-line systemic standard for progressive, symptomatic radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, and NICE recommended it in the UK. It reinforced the principle that kinase inhibitors are started for progressive or threatening disease, not for stable low-volume disease, because toxicity is significant. Later work examined lower starting doses, and selective inhibitors for RET-, NTRK- or BRAF-altered tumours now sit alongside it. For an MDT today it underpins referral of radioiodine-refractory progressive disease to thyroid oncology for a lenvatinib discussion.
